title: After Hines: day jobs and Sax Crowder's band
summary: He worked wartime day jobs and a small West Side band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Yeah, Louis Armstrong was the soloist out there. Well, what happened after you left Earl? You said you took a day gig. You said you had one day gig during your life, and that was it?
Yeah, that was -- well, I had two. Driving for Chicago Service Lines and CTA and working in the alcohol denaturing plants.
That's when things were slim in music, or --
That was during the war.
Oh, during the war.
Yeah.
Well, musically what'd you do after you left Earl?
In music? Oh, boy. That's when I went with -- who the heck was I with in the forties? I can't remember.
You had mentioned to me that you worked with Sax somebody, not Sax --
Oh, Little Sax? Robert Crowder?
Yeah.
Yeah, I worked with him. And Ruth Crowder, his wife. And Henderson Smith, trumpet player. We had a nice little four piece band. We were on the Westside.
Did you have offers to go with other big bands, after Earl broke up?
No, I never had offers to go with any other bands, big bands.
How was work in Chicago around 1940, '39?

'39 it was slow. But I was still with Earl in '39. But now in the forties, it was slow. Wasn't many gigs. Like I said, when I worked for Ruth and Sax, well, we were -- I guess we was together a couple years. And things slacked off. We was playing mostly cocktail lounges and taverns like, you know.
Where?
One place we worked was at a lake on California.
On the Westside?
On the Westside. We worked there a long time, off and on.
So it was sort of an entertaining group?
Yeah.
Singing, and things like that?
Just like, y... Joe Kelly. See, small bands have been in existence for a long time now.
